nameStory: This aquatic plant gets its name from its unique leaf arrangement - they grow in distinct whorls, like spokes on a wheel, around the stem. The 'water-milfoil' part comes from the feathery, finely-divided underwater leaves that were thought to resemble the delicate texture of the herb milfoil. It's like nature created an underwater feather duster!
description: Whorled water-milfoil is a submerged aquatic flowering plant that lives completely underwater except for its tiny flower spikes. The plant has delicate, feathery leaves that are finely divided into thread-like segments, giving it a soft, almost fuzzy appearance underwater. It can grow several feet long, creating dense underwater meadows in ponds and lakes. The distinctive whorled arrangement of its leaves makes it stand out from other aquatic plants.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery leaves arranged in whorls of 4-6 around the stem, divided into fine thread-like segments that feel soft and delicate when gently touched underwater

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny reddish or greenish flowers appear on spikes that emerge just above the water surface in summer, barely noticeable unless you look closely

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense underwater colonies with long, flexible stems that sway gracefully with water movement, rooted in bottom sediments

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, reddish-brown stems that feel firm but flexible, with distinct nodes where the whorled leaves attach

habitat: Found in shallow to moderately deep freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters with muddy or sandy bottoms where it can anchor its roots. Often grows in water 3-15 feet deep, forming underwater meadows in protected bays and coves.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from overwintering root crowns, with fresh green feathery leaves unfurling as water temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush underwater foliage and tiny flower spikes appearing above water surface in July and August.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back as temperatures cool, though some green growth may persist into early fall in warmer waters.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, surviving as dormant root systems buried in bottom sediments until spring.

funFact: This underwater plant is like a natural water filter - a single colony can process hundreds of gallons of water per day, trapping sediments in its feathery leaves and releasing oxygen that fish and other aquatic life depend on!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with the invasive Eurasian water-milfoil, but whorled water-milfoil has its leaves arranged in distinct whorls while Eurasian water-milfoil has leaves that appear more randomly spaced. Remember: 'Whorled has whorls' - if you can clearly see the spoke-like arrangement, you've likely found the native species.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of our native water-milfoils that's often mistaken for invasive species, leading to unnecessary removal efforts. It's actually beneficial to lake ecosystems and provides important habitat for fish and waterfowl, unlike some of its aggressive non-native cousins.
compareHints: Unlike the invasive Eurasian water-milfoil which has leaves scattered along the stem, whorled water-milfoil has its distinctive whorled leaf arrangement. It's very similar to northern water-milfoil (Siberian water-milfoil) but tends to have more leaves per whorl. Both native species are generally less aggressive spreaders than the invasive milfoils that can completely choke out other aquatic plants.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Eurasian water-milfoil has more finely divided leaves than most of its native relatives, with leaflets that are thread-like and numerous.
Among New England's water-milfoils, broadleaf water-milfoil stands out for having distinctly broader surface leaves compared to most relatives like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Low water-milfoil is the shortest member of its genus in New England, staying under a foot tall while Eurasian water-milfoil can reach 10 feet long.
Unlike its native milfoil cousins that stay mostly submerged, parrot's feather boldly emerges above water with bright green foliage.
Among New England's water-milfoils, Slender Water-milfoil lives up to its name with the most delicate, thread-like leaf divisions.
Unlike the aggressive Eurasian water-milfoil which forms dense mats, alternate water-milfoil grows in looser colonies and has its distinctive alternately-arranged flowers rather than whorled ones.
Siberian water-milfoil differs from other milfoils by its relatively short flower spikes and less aggressive spreading habit compared to invasive species like Eurasian water-milfoil.
